usage: the motion verb 뜨다, not 오다
지다 = sink/go down, same verb as for flowers wilting
나다 = emerge, used after clouds or rain clear
switch to 햇볕 when you mean the warmth, not the disk
examples: 아침에 해가 떠요.
The sun rises in the morning.
해가 떠요 is the fixed beginner phrase for sunrise; 떠요 comes from 뜨다.
비가 그치고 해가 났어요.
The rain stopped and the sun came out.
해가 나다 specifically means the sun reappears after bad weather.
오늘은 해가 쨍쨍해요.
The sun is blazing today.
쨍쨍 is the sound-feel adverb Koreans use for a strong, glaring sun.
nuance: 해 is the pure-Korean word for the sun as the physical disk in the sky, and it is also the everyday word for 'a day' (오늘 하루, 해가 바뀌다 = the year turns). Its near-synonym 태양(太陽) is the Sino-Korean, more scientific or literary word — you say 태양계 (solar system) and 태양이 빛나다 in writing, but in casual speech you almost always say 해. The dividing line: 해 = warm, daily, spoken; 태양 = grand, formal, written. 해 takes the motion verbs 뜨다 (rise) and 지다 (set), so the trap for English speakers is reaching for 오다/가다 by analogy with 'the sun comes up' — 해가 와요 is wrong; it must be 해가 떠요. A second pitfall is confusing 해 (the sun itself) with 햇빛 (sunlight you see) and 햇볕 (sun-warmth you feel on your skin): you do not 'look at the 해' to mean basking — that is 햇볕을 쬐다.

mistakes: Saying 해가 와요 because English says 'the sun comes up.' Korean uses the rising verb: 해가 떠요 (from 뜨다). 오다 never describes the sun.
Using 해 when you mean the warmth or the light. 해 is the disk; the warmth is 햇볕 (햇볕이 따뜻해요) and the visible light is 햇빛 (햇빛이 눈부셔요).
Reaching for 태양 in casual conversation. 태양 sounds textbook-formal; a real Korean chatting about the weather says 해 (해 떴다, 해 진다).

usage: 따뜻하다 pairs with the felt warmth of 햇볕
강하다 for intensity; 따갑다 if it stings the skin
쬐다 is the dedicated verb for soaking up sun/heat
들다 = light enters a room, 볕이 잘 드는 집 = a sunny house
examples: 오늘 햇볕이 참 따뜻해요.
The sun is really warm today.
Classic small talk; 햇볕 + 따뜻하다 is the natural warmth collocation.
햇볕이 따가워서 모자를 썼어요.
The sun stung, so I wore a hat.
따갑다 (prickly/stinging) fits strong 햇볕 better than just 강하다.
이 방은 햇볕이 잘 들어요.
This room gets good sunlight.
Real-estate phrase: 볕이 잘 들다 = a bright, sun-filled room.
nuance: 햇볕 is the sun's warmth and rays as you physically feel them on your skin — the heat, not the brightness. Its crucial near-synonym is 햇빛 (sun + 빛 light), which is the visible light you see with your eyes. The dividing line is touch vs. sight: you warm up in 햇볕 (햇볕이 따뜻하다, 햇볕을 쬐다) but you squint at 햇빛 (햇빛이 눈부시다 = the light is dazzling). 햇볕 is a compound of 해(sun) + 볕(sunlight/ray, with the ㅅ inserted as a 사이시옷), which is why the spelling ends in ㅌ — a very common spelling trap. 햇볕 takes the special verb 쬐다 (to bask/soak up), so the English-speaker pitfall is translating 'get some sun' as 햇볕을 봐요 (literally 'look at the sunshine'), which is wrong; the natural verb is 햇볕을 쬐다. Note Koreans also drop the 해 and just say 볕 (볕이 좋다).

mistakes: Spelling it 햇빛 when you mean warmth. Warmth on your skin is 햇볕(felt); the light you see is 햇빛(seen). They are different words, not spelling variants.
Writing the final consonant wrong: 햇볃 or 햇빛 instead of 햇볕. The correct ending is ㅌ (받침 티읕), pronounced [핻뼏].
Saying 햇볕을 봐요 for sunbathing. You don't 'see' the warmth; you absorb it: 햇볕을 쬐어요 (verb 쬐다).

usage: 지다 — the same setting verb as for the sun
붉다 (deep red) is the signature color of 노을
fixed compound; 아침노을 exists but is far rarer
the sky is dyed with the glow
물들다 = to be stained/dyed with color, very poetic
examples: 저녁에 노을이 정말 예뻐요.
The sunset glow is really pretty in the evening.
Everyday compliment for a beautiful sky; 노을 + 예쁘다.
하늘이 노을로 붉게 물들었어요.
The sky was dyed red with the sunset glow.
물들다 paints the whole sky — a step up in vividness from 지다.
노을 보러 바닷가에 갔어요.
We went to the beach to watch the sunset glow.
노을 보러 가다 = go specifically to see the sunset, a real outing.
nuance: 노을 is the red-orange glow that paints the sky at sunrise or (usually) sunset — the colored light on the clouds, not the sun itself. Do not confuse it with 일몰(日沒), which is the technical event of the sun sinking below the horizon (a forecast/almanac word), nor with 석양(夕陽), the Sino-Korean 'evening sun' that refers to the low sun itself rather than the painted sky. The dividing line: 노을 = the colors in the sky (pure-Korean, warm, everyday); 석양 = the setting sun disk (literary); 일몰 = the timed event (technical). 노을 takes 지다 (the same verb as 해가 지다), so 노을이 지다 = the glow comes out as the sun sets — an English speaker easily mis-hears this as 'the glow disappears,' but here 지다 means the sunset is happening, not fading. The pitfall is using 오다 (노을이 와요 ✗); the right verbs are 지다, 붉다, or the lovely 물들다 (to be dyed).

Confusing 노을 (the colored sky) with 석양 (the low evening sun) or 일몰 (the timed sunset event). 노을 is about the colors, not the sun or the clock.
Mishearing 노을이 지다 as 'the glow is fading.' Here 지다 marks the sunset happening — the glow is at its peak, not disappearing.

usage: 몰아치다 = beat down violently, the strong verb for 폭풍
불다 because 폭풍 is fundamentally about wind
지나가다 = pass through, used once it clears
fixed idiom for tense calm before trouble
examples: 오늘 밤에 폭풍이 온대요.
They say a storm is coming tonight.
-대요 reports a forecast you heard; 폭풍이 오다 is fine for 'a storm comes.'
폭풍이 불어서 나무가 쓰러졌어요.
The storm blew and trees fell over.
폭풍 + 불다 (blow) shows it is wind-driven; -어서 gives the cause.
폭풍이 몰아쳐서 배가 못 떠났어요.
The storm raged so the ship couldn't leave.
몰아치다 conveys a violent, battering storm — stronger than 불다.
nuance: 폭풍(暴風) is Sino-Korean, literally 暴 'violent' + 風 'wind' — a violent windstorm, with heavy rain implied. Its near-synonyms split by what dominates: 태풍(颱風) is a named typhoon (a specific tropical cyclone with a forecast track), 비바람 is pure-Korean 'rain-and-wind' for an ordinary nasty day, and 폭풍우(暴風雨) adds 雨 'rain' to stress the downpour. The dividing line: 폭풍 = a fierce wind event (can be metaphorical), 태풍 = the meteorological typhoon, 비바람 = everyday wet-and-windy weather. Because 風 means wind, 폭풍 naturally takes 불다 (to blow) or the intensive 몰아치다 (to rage), while 오다 also works for 'a storm comes.' The English-speaker pitfall is 폭풍이 해요 — 'storm' is a noun, never a 하다 verb. Also note 폭풍 is used metaphorically (폭풍 성장 = explosive growth, 폭풍 오열 = sobbing one's heart out), a flavor English 'storm' doesn't carry the same way.

Confusing 폭풍 with 태풍. 태풍 is a specific named typhoon with a forecast; 폭풍 is any violent windstorm (and 폭염 is a heat wave — a totally different word).
Forgetting that 폭풍 takes wind verbs. Because 風 = wind, the natural pairings are 불다 (blow) and 몰아치다 (rage), not just generic 오다.

usage: 내리다 is the standard precipitation verb
쏟아지다 for a sudden heavy burst
굵다 (thick/coarse) is the natural size word, not 크다
examples: 갑자기 우박이 내려요.
Hail is suddenly falling.
갑자기 (suddenly) is almost a fixed partner — hail is abrupt; 내리다 is the core verb.
우박이 쏟아져서 차 유리가 깨졌어요.
Hail poured down and cracked the car window.
쏟아지다 captures a violent burst; -어서 links cause to result.
주먹만 한 우박이 떨어졌어요.
Hailstones the size of fists fell.
주먹만 하다 (fist-sized) is how Koreans dramatize big hail; verb 떨어지다.
nuance: 우박 is hail — the balls of ice that fall during a storm. Do not confuse it with three look-alike winter words: 진눈깨비 is sleet (rain mixed with wet snow), 싸락눈/싸라기눈 is tiny grain-snow (much smaller, softer, and it is snow not ice), and 서리 is frost that forms on the ground. The dividing line: 우박 = hard ice balls falling from storm clouds (any season, often summer); 진눈깨비 = mushy half-rain-half-snow; 싸락눈 = fine dry snow pellets. 우박 takes 내리다 (fall), the intensive 쏟아지다 (pour), or 떨어지다 (drop), and casual 오다 works too (우박이 와요, parallel to 비가 와요). The key collocation learners miss: hail size is 굵다/굵은 우박 (coarse), not 큰 우박. The English-speaker pitfall is borrowing the wind verb 불다 — hail doesn't 'blow,' it falls: 우박이 불어요 ✗, 우박이 내려요 ✓.

mistakes: Saying 우박이 불어요 with the wind verb. Hail falls, it doesn't blow: 우박이 내려요 / 와요 / 쏟아져요.

Saying 큰 우박 for big hail. The idiomatic size word is 굵다: 우박이 굵다 / 굵은 우박이 내리다.

usage: 뜨다, the same rising verb as 해 and 달
the full moon is brilliantly bright
휘영청 is the set adverb for a dazzling full moon
둥글다 for the round shape; 동그랗다 for small round things
make a wish on the full moon
fixed cultural collocation, esp. at 정월대보름
examples: 오늘 밤에 보름달이 떴어요.
The full moon rose tonight.
보름달이 뜨다 is the base phrase; 뜨다 covers all rising sky bodies.
보름달이 휘영청 밝아요.
The full moon is brilliantly bright.
휘영청 밝다 is a near-set phrase — the poetic way to say a full moon is dazzling.
보름달을 보면서 소원을 빌었어요.
I made a wish while looking at the full moon.
소원을 빌다 (make a wish) is the Chuseok/대보름 custom learners should know.
nuance: 보름달 is the full moon — a pure-Korean compound of 보름 (the 15th day of the lunar month, i.e. mid-month) + 달 (moon). Its opposite is 초승달 (crescent moon), and its plain superordinate is just 달 (moon). The cultural weight matters: the full moon is tied to 추석 (Chuseok, the harvest festival) and especially 정월대보름 (the first full moon of the lunar year), when Koreans make wishes — so 보름달 carries warm festive connotations a bare 'full moon' lacks in English. It takes 뜨다 (rise) like all sky bodies, and its signature description is 휘영청 밝다 (brilliantly bright). The English-speaker pitfalls: (1) reaching for 오다 — 보름달이 와요 ✗, it must be 보름달이 떠요; (2) assuming 'full' is a separate adjective — there is no 가득한 달; the fullness is baked into the single word 보름달.

mistakes: Saying 보름달이 와요. The moon rises, so use 뜨다: 보름달이 떠요. 오다 doesn't apply to moons.
Confusing 보름달 (full moon) with 초승달 (crescent). 보름(mid-month, round) vs 초승(start of the lunar month, thin sliver) are opposites.
Trying to build 'full moon' from an adjective + 달 (e.g. 가득한 달). It is one fixed word, 보름달, where 보름 already means the 15th/full phase.

usage: 가늘다 (slender) for the thin sliver shape
눈썹 같다 is the classic shape metaphor
걸리다 = to be hung/caught, poetic for a sliver moon
examples: 하늘에 초승달이 떴어요.
A crescent moon rose in the sky.
Base sentence; 초승달 + 뜨다 just like any moon.
초승달이 눈썹처럼 가늘어요.
The crescent moon is thin like an eyebrow.
눈썹처럼 가늘다 — the standard simile Koreans use for a slim crescent.
서쪽 하늘에 초승달이 걸려 있어요.
A crescent moon hangs in the western sky.
걸려 있다 (is hanging) gives a still, picturesque image.
nuance: 초승달 is the thin crescent moon seen just after the new moon — a pure-Korean compound from 초승 (the very start of the lunar month) + 달 (moon). It is the direct opposite of 보름달 (full moon). Be careful with two relatives: 그믐달 is also a crescent but the waning one seen at the END of the lunar month (just before the new moon), and the shapes face opposite ways; 반달 is the half moon, a separate phase in between. The dividing line: 초승달 = waxing sliver at the month's start; 그믐달 = waning sliver at the month's end; 반달 = half; 보름달 = full. It takes 뜨다 (rise) and is described with 가늘다 (thin) — the trademark image is 눈썹 같은 초승달 (eyebrow-shaped crescent). English-speaker pitfalls: using 오다 (초승달이 와요 ✗ → 떠요 ✓), and assuming any thin crescent is 초승달 when a waning one is properly 그믐달.

Using 크다/작다 for its shape. A crescent's defining trait is thinness — describe it with 가늘다 (가는 초승달), not size words.

usage: 반짝이다 is the signature twinkle verb
쏟아지다 paints a sky overflowing with stars
아래 = beneath; a set romantic/poetic phrase
물들다 = to be steeped/dyed in the light, literary
examples: 밤하늘에 별빛이 반짝여요.
Starlight twinkles in the night sky.
별빛 + 반짝이다 is the core, must-know pairing for twinkling light.
시골이라 별빛이 쏟아져요.
Out in the countryside, starlight pours down.
쏟아지다 conveys a dazzling, dense field of stars — far from city lights.
별빛 아래에서 이야기를 나눴어요.
We talked under the starlight.
별빛 아래(서) is a fixed atmospheric phrase for a romantic night scene.
nuance: 별빛 is starlight — a transparent compound of 별 (star) + 빛 (light), where the ㅅ is a 사이시옷 inserted between the two nouns (so it is written 별빛, pronounced [별삗]). Distinguish it cleanly from its sibling 달빛 (moonlight) and from plain 별 (the star itself): 별 is the body you point at, 별빛 is the light it casts. Because 빛 means light, the natural verbs are 반짝이다 (twinkle), 빛나다 (shine), and the vivid 쏟아지다 (pour), and the most idiomatic location phrase is 별빛 아래 (under the starlight). The big English-speaker pitfall is the verb 오다: light does not 'come' in Korean, so 별빛이 와요 ✗; light 반짝여요/비쳐요/쏟아져요. usage: 비치다 = to shine/be reflected onto a surface
the moonlight is soft and mellow
은은하다 is the trademark adjective for gentle moonlight
환하다 (brightly lit) for a bright moonlit night
set phrase for a calm, romantic night
examples: 오늘 밤 달빛이 환해요.
The moonlight is bright tonight.
환하다 fits a clear, well-lit moonlit night; 달빛 + 환하다.
창문으로 달빛이 비쳐요.
Moonlight shines in through the window.
비치다 needs a surface/opening the light falls on — here 창문으로(through the window).
달빛이 은은하게 비쳐요.
The moonlight shines softly and mellow.
은은하다, the signature 'soft glow' word, distinguishes gentle moonlight from harsh light.
nuance: 달빛 is moonlight — a compound of 달 (moon) + 빛 (light) with the same 사이시옷 as 별빛 (written 달빛, pronounced [달삗]). The natural verb is 비치다 (to shine onto / be cast on a surface), which is why 창문으로 달빛이 비치다 (moonlight shines through the window) is so common — 비치다 implies the light lands somewhere. usage: snow comes down in big thick flakes
펑펑 is the set adverb for heavy fluffy snow
쏟아지다 for a sudden, abundant snowfall
소복이 쌓이다 = accumulate in a soft mound
examples: 밖에 함박눈이 와요.
Big snowflakes are falling outside.
함박눈 + 오다, exactly parallel to 비가 와요/눈이 와요.
함박눈이 펑펑 내려요.
Big fluffy snowflakes are coming down thickly.
펑펑 내리다 is the near-fixed phrase for heavy, fat-flake snow.
하룻밤 새 함박눈이 소복이 쌓였어요.
Overnight, big snowflakes piled up in a soft mound.
소복이 쌓이다 describes the gentle, deep accumulation 함박눈 is loved for.
nuance: 함박눈 is big, fluffy snowflakes that fall thick and slow — the picturesque snow Koreans adore. Its key contrast is 싸락눈 (or 싸라기눈), the fine dry snow pellets that fall in very cold, hard weather: 함박눈 = large soft flakes (often near 0°C, sticks and piles up beautifully); 싸락눈 = tiny gritty grains (bitter cold, doesn't stick well). Also distinguish 진눈깨비 (sleet — wet, slushy rain mixed with snow, which Koreans dislike). The name comes from 함박 (a big wooden bowl / the large 함박꽃 peony blossom), so 함박눈 literally evokes 'bowl-big / peony-big snow' — the same 함박 in 함박웃음 (a big beaming smile). It takes the snow verbs 오다 (casual) and 내리다 (standard), and its trademark adverb is 펑펑 (펑펑 내리다 = pouring down in fat flakes). English-speaker pitfalls: using the wind verb 불다 (함박눈이 불어요 ✗ → 와요/내려요 ✓), and treating 함박 as if it described size with 큰 (don't say 큰 눈; the single word 함박눈 already means 'big-flake snow').

usage: 끼다 is the dedicated verb for clouds/fog covering the sky
몰려오다 = surge in as a mass, for an approaching storm
짙다 (dense, deep-colored) for heavy cloud cover
드리우다 = to hang/cast over, also metaphorical for gloom
examples: 하늘에 먹구름이 꼈어요.
Dark clouds gathered in the sky.
먹구름 + 끼다 is the core pairing; 꼈어요 is the past of 끼다.
먹구름이 몰려와서 곧 비가 올 것 같아요.
Dark clouds rolled in, so it looks like rain soon.
몰려오다 shows the clouds advancing as a front; -ㄹ 것 같다 makes a guess.
회사 앞날에 먹구름이 드리웠어요.
Dark clouds loomed over the company's future.
Metaphorical use: 먹구름이 드리우다 = trouble/gloom looms — a flavor English shares.
nuance: 먹구름 is a dark, gray-black rain cloud — a pure-Korean compound of 먹 (ink, the black inkstick used in calligraphy) + 구름 (cloud), so literally 'ink cloud.' Contrast it with plain 구름 (any cloud, neutral) and with 뭉게구름 (big white fluffy cumulus, a fair-weather cloud): 먹구름 specifically signals rain or a storm is coming, while 뭉게구름 signals a nice day. The defining verb is 끼다 — the special verb for clouds, fog, or haze settling over the sky (구름이 끼다, 안개가 끼다), so the sky 'wears' clouds rather than having them 'come.' It also takes 몰려오다 (roll in) and 드리우다 (loom), and 먹구름 is freely metaphorical for impending bad news (앞날에 먹구름이 끼다). The main English-speaker pitfall is 먹구름이 와요 (by analogy with 비가 와요 'rain comes') — clouds don't 'come,' they gather: 먹구름이 껴요 ✓. Don't strip it to plain 구름 when you mean ominous clouds; the darkness and warning are in the 먹.

usage: 맞추다 for setting an AC, oven, or bath to a target
examples: 방 온도가 딱 좋아요.
The room temperature is just right.
딱 좋다 (just right) is the everyday comfort phrase; 온도 covers a room.
에어컨 온도를 26도에 맞췄어요.
I set the AC to 26 degrees.
온도를 맞추다 = set a device's temperature — a very common daily action.
아기 온도를 재 봤어요.
I took the baby's temperature.
온도 also covers body temperature; 온도를 재다 = to measure/take a temperature
nuance: 온도(溫度) is Sino-Korean — 溫 'warm' + 度 'degree' — the general word for temperature of air, water, a room, an oven, anything you can read on a thermometer. Its near-synonyms are narrower: 기온(氣溫, 'air-temperature') is specifically the outdoor air temperature in a weather report, and 체온(體溫, 'body-temperature') is body heat. The dividing line: use 온도 broadly (방 온도, 물 온도), but switch to 기온 for the weather forecast (오늘 기온이 영하예요) and 체온 for a fever (체온이 38도예요). Because it is measured in degrees on a scale, the correct adjectives are 높다/낮다 (high/low), and it moves with 올라가다/내려가다. The number-one English-speaker pitfall is 온도가 커요/작아요 — English says 'high/low temperature,' and Korean agrees: it must be 온도가 높아요/낮아요, never 크다/작다. A second is using 온도 for the outdoor weather when 기온 is what newscasters say.

usage: 떨어지다 (plunge) is more vivid than 내려가다 for crossing zero
examples: 오늘 아침은 영하 5도예요.
This morning it's minus five degrees.
Word order to memorize: 영하 + number + 도. Never 5도 영하.
기온이 영하로 떨어졌어요.
The temperature dropped below zero.
영하로 떨어지다 = the reading plunges past zero; 로 marks the endpoint.
내일은 영하권 추위가 와요.
Subzero cold is coming tomorrow.
영하권 (the subzero zone) is how forecasters frame a cold snap.
nuance: 영하(零下) is Sino-Korean — 零 'zero' + 下 'below' — meaning below 0°C. Its exact opposite is 영상(零上, 'above zero'), used for plus temperatures (영상 3도 = +3°C). The crucial structural fact, opposite to English, is word order: the marker comes BEFORE the number, so 'minus five degrees' is 영하 5도 (literally 'below-zero five degrees'), never 5도 영하. English speakers also say 'negative five' / 'minus five,' but Korean does not use 마이너스 in weather speech — it is always 영하. 영하 most often appears in winter forecasts and pairs with 떨어지다 (plunge below) and 내려가다 (drop), plus the handy forecaster word 영하권 (the subzero range). The pitfalls: (1) putting the number first (5도 영하 ✗); (2) confusing 영하 (below zero) with 영상 (above zero) — they look and sound similar but are opposites; (3) saying 마이너스 5도 in everyday weather talk, which sounds like a math/English calque rather than natural 영하 5도.

usage: 들다, the set verb (as for sickness/famine 'setting in')
계속되다 for a prolonged dry spell
풀리다 = to be relieved/loosened, when rain finally comes
examples: 올해는 가뭄이 심해요.
The drought is severe this year.
가뭄 + 심하다, the everyday way to say a bad drought.
비가 안 와서 가뭄이 들었어요.
A drought set in because it didn't rain.
가뭄이 들다 (a drought sets in) — note 들다, not 오다; -어서 gives the cause.
단비가 내려서 가뭄이 풀렸어요.
A welcome rain fell and the drought broke.
가뭄이 풀리다 = the drought lifts; 단비(welcome rain) is its natural rescuer.
nuance: 가뭄 is a drought — a pure-Korean noun for a long stretch with little or no rain. It is the direct opposite of 장마 (the summer monsoon rainy season), and learners often pair the two. The defining verb is 들다, which here means 'to set in / take hold' — the same 들다 used when an illness or a famine grips (병이 들다, 흉년이 들다) — so 가뭄이 들다 frames the drought as something that settles over the land, not something that 'arrives.' It is described with 심하다 (severe) and 계속되다 (continues), and lifts with 풀리다 (가뭄이 풀리다 = the drought breaks), often thanks to 단비 (a welcome, much-needed rain). The English-speaker pitfall is 가뭄이 와요 (by analogy with 'a drought comes' / 비가 와요) — a drought doesn't 'come,' it 들어요. Also keep 가뭄 (no rain, dryness) distinct from 장마 (too much rain): they are opposite weather problems, and mixing the verbs (가뭄이 오다 / 장마가 들다) sounds wrong.
